bullets: Periodicity across period 3 and down groups 2 and 17, then transition metals: colour, complexes, catalysis - and why zinc does not make the cut
slides.heading: JC H2 chemistry — inorganic: periodicity, groups and transition metals
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we read the periodic table as a set of trends with reasons - radius, melting point and ionisation energy across period 3, reactivity and oxidising power down the groups, and the d-orbital story that defines a transition metal.

bullets: Explain the period 3 trends in atomic radius, melting point and first ionisation energy, including the two ionisation-energy dips
Explain why reactivity rises down group 2 while oxidising power falls down group 17
Define a transition metal by its ions, explain complex formation and colour, and judge whether zinc qualifies
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the three goals aloud slowly and tell the class: keep these in mind, because our exit ticket at the end will ask you to do exactly these things, including spotting the trap that zinc must be a transition metal.

bullets: Zinc sits in the d-block of the periodic table, between copper and gallium
Does its address in the table settle the question, or does the definition ask something else?
slides.heading: Zinc sits in the d-block. Is it a transition metal?
slides.notes: Ask the class to commit to a guess before any definitions: d-block address, transition metal, yes or no? Take two or three answers, then say: hold them, because the trap scene of the lesson settles this question completely.

bullets: Every periodic trend in this lesson is explained the same way: nuclear charge, atomic radius and shielding decide how strongly electrons are held, gained or lost
Transition-metal behaviour comes from a partially filled d subshell: colour, complexes, variable oxidation states and catalysis all trace back to it
slides.heading: One idea, eight scenes: trends with reasons, metals with d-orbitals
slides.notes: Say this part slowly, because it is the big idea of the whole lesson: trends are never memorised lists - each one is charge, size and shielding, and the d-subshell story is the same idea one shell deeper.

bullets: Across period 3 the nuclear charge rises from sodium to argon while the outer electrons stay in the same shell, so the pull on each electron grows
Shielding barely changes across the period, so atomic radius falls steadily from sodium to argon
slides.heading: Across period 3, atoms shrink
slides.notes: Follow the probe left to right and narrate the state change: same shell, rising nuclear charge, atoms drawn smaller and smaller. Say: it is the extra protons, not extra shells, that shrink the atom.

bullets: Melting point follows structure: sodium, magnesium and aluminium are metallic, silicon is a giant covalent lattice, and phosphorus to argon are simple molecular
The peak sits at silicon because melting a giant covalent lattice means breaking strong covalent bonds, not weak forces between molecules
slides.heading: Melting point tells the structure story
slides.notes: Narrate the bars in order: modest metals, the silicon peak, then the fall to the simple molecular elements. Say: read the structure off the melting point before you read anything else.

bullets: First ionisation energy rises across period 3 as nuclear charge grows and radius falls, so the outer electron is held ever tighter
Two dips break the rise: magnesium to aluminium (the electron leaves a higher-energy 3p orbital) and phosphorus to sulphur (paired-electron repulsion in the 3p orbital)
slides.heading: First ionisation energy: the rise, and two dips
slides.notes: Walk the rising curve, then pause at each dip and ask why before revealing it. Say: a dip never breaks the trend - it refines it, and each dip has an orbital reason.

bullets: Down group 2 the atoms get larger and the outer electrons sit further from the nucleus under more shielding, so they are lost more easily
Reactivity with water climbs from magnesium to barium: magnesium reacts slowly with cold water, barium vigorously
slides.heading: Down group 2: reactivity climbs
slides.notes: Narrate the climb down the group: bigger atoms, more shielding, electrons lost more readily. Say: reactivity down group 2 is atomic size and shielding doing the work.

bullets: Down group 17 the atoms get larger, so an incoming electron is gained further from the nucleus and held less strongly
Oxidising power falls from chlorine to iodine: chlorine displaces bromide and iodide, but iodine displaces neither
slides.heading: Down group 17: oxidising power falls
slides.notes: Follow the oxidising power falling down the group and tie it to the displacement reactions. Say: the halogen that wants the electron most is the smallest one at the top.

bullets: Transition-metal ions are coloured because partially filled d orbitals split into two energy levels and electrons absorb visible light jumping between them
The colour depends on the metal, its oxidation state and the ligands present - change any of them and the colour changes
slides.heading: Colour comes from partially filled d-orbitals
slides.notes: Point at the split d-orbitals and the absorbed colour. Say: no partially filled d subshell means no d-d transitions - keep that sentence ready for the zinc trap at the end.

bullets: Ligands donate lone pairs into empty metal orbitals, forming coordinate bonds in a complex ion such as [Cu(H2O)6]2+

Transition metals make good catalysts because they can flip between oxidation states, as iron(II) and iron(III) do, or provide a surface for reactants to adsorb onto, as iron does in the Haber process
slides.heading: Ligands crowd the metal; catalysts flip oxidation states
slides.notes: Narrate the ligands crowding in around the metal ion, then the catalyst flipping oxidation states. Say: variable oxidation states and complex formation are the two signatures of transition-metal behaviour.

bullets: A transition metal is defined by forming at least one stable ion with a partially filled d subshell - d-block position alone is not the definition
Zinc forms only Zn2+, which is 3d10: completely filled, so zinc shows none of the colour or complex behaviour that needs a d-orbital gap
slides.heading: A common mistake: zinc is a transition metal
slides.notes: Slow down for the trap scene. Say: the definition is about the ion's d subshell, not about where the element sits in the table - scene s6 already told us why that matters.

bullets: Step 1: magnesium to aluminium - magnesium's outer electron leaves the 3s orbital, aluminium's leaves the higher-energy 3p orbital, so less energy is needed even though nuclear charge has risen
Step 2: phosphorus to sulphur - phosphorus has three unpaired 3p electrons, sulphur has one paired 3p orbital, and the paired electrons repel, so one is removed more easily
slides.heading: Worked example: explaining the two ionisation-energy dips
slides.notes: Talk through the two dips slowly and name the orbital reason for each as you write it; say: nuclear charge rises at both steps, so the dips must come from the orbitals, not from the trend reversing.

bullets: Explain, using charge, radius and shielding, why the first ionisation energy of potassium is lower than that of sodium
Careful - a classmate says: Zinc is a transition metal because it sits in the d-block. Explain to them what the definition of a transition metal actually requires
slides.heading: Your turn: explain, then correct
slides.notes: Give pairs three minutes, then cold-call one pair on each part: press them on bigger atom, more shielding, weaker hold first, then on the exact sentence they used to talk their classmate out of the claim: Zinc is a transition metal because it sits in the d-block.

bullets: On your own: chlorine displaces bromide from solution but bromine does not displace chloride. Explain this using oxidising power down group 17
Watch out for the trap one last time: Zinc is a transition metal because it sits in the d-block. Say what Zn2+ has in its 3d subshell, and what that means for the definition
slides.heading: Exit ticket: show what you know
slides.notes: Collect these before anyone leaves and say: I am looking for oxidising power falling down the group in your first answer and one clear sentence about the full 3d subshell in your second. Anyone repeating the claim Zinc is a transition metal because it sits in the d-block. needs the trap scene again.
